opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think there's a clean answer. Granular skill benchmarks have a lot going for them. They're cheap to run, the scoring tends to be unambiguous, and when a model fails you can usually say pretty precisely what it failed at. That's useful if you're trying to track a specific capability, like multi-step arithmetic or reading a particular kind of code, and you want a clean signal over time.

The problem is that what we actually care about, especially from a safety or forecasting perspective, is whether these systems can do economically meaningful or dangerous things in the world. Those tasks don't decompose neatly into the skills we happen to have benchmarks for. A model can look great on a dozen narrow tests and then fall apart on a realistic task because it can't recover from its own mistakes, or it loses track of what it was doing three hours in, or it doesn't know when to check its work. A lot of what matters is in the glue between skills, and narrow benchmarks mostly don't measure the glue.

So I've moved toward thinking realistic, longer-horizon tasks deserve more weight than they've historically gotten, even though they're expensive and messy. You need humans to build them, often humans to baseline them so you know how hard they actually are, and grading can be subjective. You also get fewer data points, so your error bars are wider. But the construct validity is much better. When a model succeeds at something that takes a skilled person several hours, that tells you something fairly direct about what it can do.

The way I'd frame the trade-off is that granular benchmarks are good for diagnosis and realistic tasks are good for measurement of the thing you care about. Ideally you have both, and you use the realistic tasks to check whether gains on the granular ones actually transfer. If they don't, that's a sign your narrow benchmarks are measuring something that's become decoupled from real capability, which happens a lot once people start optimizing for them.

One more thing I'd add is that saturation pushes you toward realism over time. Narrow benchmarks get saturated quickly, and you end up in a treadmill of making harder narrow tests. Anchoring to realistic tasks, and to something like how long a task takes a human, gives you a scale that doesn't top out as fast and is easier to interpret for people outside the field.

r001.rationale: It contrasts precise, diagnostic narrow benchmarks with realistic tasks that better indicate what systems can do in the world.

r002.rationale: It describes models failing realistic tasks despite strong narrow scores, but does not say that inconsistent capabilities prevent an especially crisp understanding of their skills.

r003.rationale: It explicitly gives realistic, longer-horizon tasks more weight for measuring economically meaningful or dangerous capabilities, while retaining granular benchmarks for diagnosis.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and I'd say my view has shifted over time. There's a real tension here, and I don't think either side of it is just obviously correct.

The case for granular skill benchmarks is that they're interpretable. If you have a benchmark that measures, say, how well a model can do multi-step arithmetic, or how well it can follow a long chain of instructions, and the model gets 70% on it, you have a pretty clear sense of what that means. You can diagnose failures. You can say "the model is bad at X" and that's actually a meaningful statement that people can act on. And they're cheap to construct and cheap to run, so you can iterate quickly.

The problem is that the thing we actually care about is almost never the granular skill. We care about whether the system can do useful work in the world, or whether it's dangerous, or whether it can meaningfully accelerate research. And it turns out that the mapping from individual skills to real-world capability is really unclear. You can have a model that aces a bunch of component skill tests and then just falls apart when you give it a messy, long-horizon task where it has to figure out what the task even is, recover from its own mistakes, and manage context over hours. Conversely, sometimes models do surprisingly well on realistic tasks even when they look weak on some decomposed skill, because they find a different route to the answer than a human would.

So realistic tasks are closer to the thing you care about, and that's a big deal. If your question is "can this model do the job of a junior software engineer," the most direct way to find out is to give it tasks that look like what a junior software engineer actually does. The downside is that they're expensive, they're noisy, they're often hard to grade, and when a model fails you frequently don't know why. Was it the planning? Was it a tool-use issue? Did it just not understand the codebase? You get a number, and the number is meaningful, but it's not very diagnostic.

The way I've come to think about it is that these aren't really substitutes, they're serving different functions. Realistic tasks are the thing you should be anchoring on for the actual question of "what can this system do." They're your ground truth. Granular benchmarks are more like instruments that help you understand the structure of the capability. The failure mode I worry about is when people treat the granular benchmarks as if they were the ground truth, because they're easy and they produce clean numbers, and then the field optimizes toward them and the numbers stop meaning what they used to mean.

The other thing I'd add is that "realistic" is doing a lot of work in that phrase, and it's harder to achieve than people think. A lot of tasks that are presented as realistic are actually pretty sanitized. The task is well-specified, the environment is clean, there's a clear success criterion. Real work usually isn't like that. So I'm somewhat skeptical of a lot of what gets called realistic evaluation, and I think the field should be more honest about the ways in which our "realistic" tasks are still quite artificial.

If I had to give a practical recommendation, I'd say: invest heavily in a small number of genuinely realistic, high-effort evaluations that you treat as your real signal, and then use granular benchmarks as a fast, cheap way to explore the space and generate hypotheses about why the realistic evals are coming out the way they are. But don't confuse the two.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts granular benchmarks’ interpretability and diagnostic value with the unclear mapping from those skills to useful real-world capability.

r002.rationale: It describes models that excel on component tests but fail at messy tasks, and models that succeed at realistic tasks despite weak decomposed scores, showing why their skills are hard to characterize crisply.

r003.rationale: It says realistic tasks should anchor judgments about what a system can do, while granular benchmarks should serve as supporting diagnostic instruments.

astra-6.text:
I think they serve different purposes. If you want to understand why a model succeeds or fails, it’s useful to isolate particular skills. You can make the evaluation more controlled, and you can distinguish capabilities that might otherwise get bundled together in a single score. But then there’s a question of whether those skills actually translate into doing something useful in the world.

Realistic tasks give you a more direct handle on that, but they’re harder to interpret. If a model fails at a long task, maybe it lacks some crucial knowledge, or maybe it just made one mistake early on and couldn’t recover. Those are pretty different limitations, and the overall success rate doesn’t necessarily distinguish them.

So I’d want both, and I’d especially want to study the relationship between them. If performance on your granular benchmarks improves, does that predict better performance on the realistic tasks? If it doesn’t, that’s a reason to reconsider what your benchmarks are measuring. I wouldn’t treat either kind of evaluation as a complete picture on its own.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts controlled, skill-specific evaluations with realistic tasks that more directly show usefulness in the world, while noting that realistic-task outcomes are harder to interpret.

r002.rationale: It notes that realistic-task failures can have different causes, but does not say neural networks’ inconsistent capabilities prevent a crisp understanding of their skills.

r003.rationale: The response recommends using both kinds of evaluation and studying their relationship; it does not favor broader deployment-relevant assessments over granular evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they serve different purposes. If you want to understand why a model succeeds or fails, it’s useful to isolate particular skills. You can make more controlled comparisons, and you have a better chance of figuring out what an improvement actually means. But there’s a danger in assuming that doing well on each of those pieces means the model can put them together to accomplish something useful.

With more realistic tasks, you’re asking something closer to the question you ultimately care about: can this system actually do the work? But then a failure can be hard to interpret. Did it lack the relevant knowledge, misunderstand the task, or make one mistake early on that derailed everything else?

So I’d want both, ideally connected to each other. Use realistic tasks to measure whether the system can accomplish the objective, and more granular evaluations to investigate what’s driving that performance. And be careful about the scope of the conclusion: a benchmark can give you evidence about a capability without establishing that the system can reliably exercise it in every setting where it matters.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts granular evaluations, which help isolate skills and interpret improvements, with realistic tasks, which show whether the system can accomplish useful work.

r002.rationale: It says failures on realistic tasks can be hard to interpret, but does not attribute this to neural networks’ inconsistent capabilities or say that this prevents a crisp understanding of their skills.

r003.rationale: The response recommends using both realistic tasks and granular evaluations; it does not favor broader deployment-relevant assessments over granular evaluations.
